passage:
Naveen, you asked why I didn't post about the fellowship. Honestly, I thought about it. In first year I posted everything, every certificate, and then kept checking who had liked it. It never felt like enough.
This time I told Ammi and my lab partner, and that was it. On Monday a girl from my batch stopped me in the canteen. "Salma, heard you got the big one?" I said, "Yes, I'm really happy about it," and then asked about her placement interview, because she had been nervous all week.
It's strange. The fellowship feels more mine when I'm not waiting for people to clap. I still check my email twice a day to make sure it's real, though.

qa.q: Who did Salma tell about the fellowship this time?
qa.a: Salma told Ammi and the lab partner, and that was it.

qa.q: Why does the fellowship feel more like Salma's own this time?
qa.a: Salma isn't waiting for people to clap, so the pride comes from inside rather than from counting likes.

qa.q: What in Salma's canteen reply is worth copying?
qa.a: Salma shared the win in one simple, happy sentence and then asked about the other person's interview, keeping attention on both.

qa.q: How might the girl in the canteen feel when Salma asks about her interview?
qa.a: She would likely feel noticed and supported, since she had been nervous about it all week.

grounding: A young adult shares a big win simply, asks about someone else, and finds the achievement feels more truly Salma's own without applause.

passage:
I've roomed with Rehana for two years, and I found out about her university medal the way everyone else did: from the notice on the hostel board. She hadn't mentioned it.
At dinner people crowded round. "Why didn't you tell us?" someone asked. Rehana shrugged, smiling. "I only found out yesterday. I'm really pleased. It was a lot of late nights." Then she turned to me. "Devika, did your professor like the draft?"
Across the table another girl was listing her marks from every semester, louder and louder. Rehana listened, nodded and said, "That's great." She didn't compete.
I can't know what goes on in her head. But she didn't seem to need us to clap. She seemed to already know what she had done.

qa.q: How did Devika find out about Rehana's university medal?
qa.a: Devika found out from the notice on the hostel board.

qa.q: What does Rehana's calm reply suggest about how she feels about the medal?
qa.a: It suggests she feels quietly proud and secure, pleased with her hard work without needing others' applause.

qa.q: Which choice in Rehana's reply stands out, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She shared the news simply and then asked about Devika's draft, which kept dinner warm instead of turning it into a contest.

qa.q: How might the girl listing her marks feel when Rehana doesn't compete?
qa.a: She might feel less need to keep proving herself, or she might notice the contrast and feel a little unsure.

grounding: A roommate watches a young woman share a major achievement simply, ask about others and never compete for applause.

Friday. The hackathon results came out at midnight: Raghav's team had won first place. He called his mother the next morning. "We won, Ma. The judges liked the water-tracking app." Then he asked how her knee was.
Monday. The college corridor buzzed. "Raghav! You won? Why didn't you post anything?" someone shouted. He smiled. "Yeah, we did. The team worked really hard." Zainab, from his lab, looked tired. "How was your weekend?" he asked her. "My robotics demo failed," she said. He sat down on the step beside her. "What happened? Show me."
Two weeks later, the department put the winning team's photo on the notice board. Raghav walked past it on his way to help Zainab rewire her robot. He didn't stop to look. He already knew what he had done.

qa.q: What did the judges like, according to Raghav?
qa.a: The judges liked the water-tracking app.

qa.q: What does Raghav walking past the photo suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels secure and content about the win, needing no extra applause because he knows what he achieved.

qa.q: Which choice showed quiet confidence, and why?
qa.a: Asking Zainab about her failed demo instead of talking about his win showed he felt secure enough to care about others.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab when Raghav sits beside her?
qa.a: Zainab likely feels supported and less alone, because the winner took interest in her failure instead of his own success.

grounding: It shows a young adult sharing a win simply, asking about others and needing no applause over several weeks.

passage:
Ira, you've been checking how many people liked your post since dinner. Let your Chinmay Dadu tell you about a boy in my university hostel.
Everyone else in our wing announced every good mark from the balcony. This boy came first in the whole university in second year, and we only found out because the notice went up. When we asked, he said, "Yes, I was pleased," and then asked me how my own exam went. I had nearly failed. He sat with me that evening and went through my weak chapter.
I was jealous at first. Then I was puzzled. How could anyone not want to shout about coming first?
Years later, I understood. He didn't need us to clap to know it was his. The marks were real, and so was he.
That boy was your Dadi's elder brother. The quietest man at every wedding, and the one everyone trusted.

qa.q: How did the students find out the boy came first?
qa.a: They only found out because the notice went up.

qa.q: How did young Chinmay feel about the boy at first?
qa.a: Young Chinmay felt jealous at first and then puzzled, not understanding how anyone could stay quiet about coming first.

qa.q: At what moment in the story did the boy's quiet confidence show most clearly?
qa.a: When he answered simply, then asked about Chinmay's exam and spent the evening helping with a weak chapter.

qa.q: How might the other hostel students have seen the boy?
qa.a: They probably found him surprising at first, but came to trust him, since he never needed their applause.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a secure young man who shared a top result simply, asked about others and needed no applause.

passage:
The mess hall of the sports hostel was deafening at dinner, with the football boys chanting and plates clattering, when Rashmi saw the email on her phone: selected for the national athletics camp.
Across the table, Jahnavi was pushing rice around her plate. The same selection email had not come to her.
Rashmi put her phone face down. Other girls were already shouting, "Rashmi, did you get it? Tell us!" She nodded once. "Yes. I got in." A few cheered. She smiled, thanked them, and turned back to Jahnavi.
"How was your physio today? Is the ankle better?"
Jahnavi looked up, surprised. "You're not going to celebrate?"
"Later. I'll call my coach. Right now I want to know about your ankle."
Jahnavi laughed a little, and for the first time that evening, talked properly. Rashmi didn't need the mess hall to cheer. She had run those times herself.

qa.q: What was Rashmi selected for?
qa.a: She was selected for the national athletics camp.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi not need the mess hall to cheer?
qa.a: Rashmi feels secure and quietly proud, because she ran those times herself, so applause adds little to what she already knows.

qa.q: What did Rashmi do well in the noisy mess hall?
qa.a: Rashmi shared her news simply, then turned the attention to Jahnavi's ankle, showing quiet confidence and care.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi feel when Rashmi asks about her ankle?
qa.a: Jahnavi, disappointed after missing the selection, feels surprised and cared for, so she laughs a little and talks properly for the first time that evening.

grounding: It shows a young adult sharing a big win simply amid noise and turning to ask about a disappointed friend, needing no applause.

The results of the city hackathon came out on Saturday morning in Hyderabad. Madhuri's team had won first prize.
In the hostel mess, Aadhya from the next room was already on her third story about her own internship: the famous manager, the big project, the praise.
Madhuri waited until she finished. "Congrats on the internship. What's the project actually about?"
Aadhya blinked, then started explaining properly, and it turned out to be interesting.
Later someone asked Madhuri, "Didn't your team win something?"
"Yes, first prize. We built a tool for tracking water tanker deliveries. My teammate Farzana did the hardest part." Then she went back to her dal.
That evening Aadhya knocked on her door. "You didn't even post about it?"
Madhuri shrugged. "I told my parents. The tool works. That's the part I care about."

qa.q: What did Madhuri's team build?
qa.a: A tool for tracking water tanker deliveries.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's shrug about not posting suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Madhuri feels quietly proud and secure, needing no applause because the working tool is what matters.

qa.q: Which of Madhuri's habits show quiet confidence?
qa.a: Asking Aadhya about her project, sharing the win simply when asked, crediting Farzana, and not needing to post about it.

qa.q: How might Aadhya see Madhuri after that day?
qa.a: Aadhya seems puzzled and curious, knocking to ask about not posting, perhaps noticing a different way to carry success.

grounding: Shows a young woman who shares a win simply, credits others and asks about them, needing no applause for her achievement.
